intro: A cello phrase reaches towards the woodwind, and four notes open a wound that the whole prelude keeps touching. Wagner makes an orchestra yearn through the smallest possible step: one semitone.

sections.label: Intro · Cellos reach into silence
sections.mNote: Cellos and woodwind exchange three rising phrases, separated by rests

sections.label: A · The strings join the phrases
sections.mNote: The violin melody continues over moving lower strings

sections.label: B · Woodwind carry the rising line
sections.mNote: The short rising melody passes through woodwind and strings

sections.label: Dev · Strings climb beneath the woodwind
sections.mNote: Quick string figures climb beneath longer wind notes

sections.label: C · The whole orchestra presses upwards
sections.mNote: Brass and woodwind rise above rushing strings

sections.label: Link · The brass fall silent
sections.mNote: The timpani roll on E beneath dwindling string phrases

sections.label: Coda · The concert ending
sections.mNote: The orchestra closes the prelude without the sailor’s song

cues.title: Four notes over the cellos
cues.text: The cellos rise from A to F. Woodwind enter with F–B–D♯–G♯, the Tristan chord. It moves into E7, a chord that points towards A minor. The expected arrival never comes. A rest opens beneath the unfinished phrase.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel, Vorspiel und Isoldens Liebestod, plate Part. B. 1544, p. 3, opening bars: https://hdl.handle.net/1802/13070. University of Texas analysis and score examples, https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude.php and https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/motive1-3.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A semitone at a time
cues.text: G♯–A–A♯–B: the opening woodwind line climbs by semitones. Wagner repeats the shape at new pitches, each attempt reaching a little farther. These tiny steps give the prelude its ache; even a rising melody can seem unable to leave the spot.
cues.evidence: University of Texas, Tristan Prelude analysis, first seventeen bars and the rising desire motif: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude.php. This note describes the opening motif across its successive statements.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The strings carry on
cues.text: The violin melody continues where the opening phrases kept stopping. Violas and cellos move beneath it; the next idea begins before the previous one has quite let go. Wagner also asks the violins to play a rising passage on the G string, keeping its dark colour as it climbs.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 3–4; p. 4 marks the rising first- and second-violin figures ‘auf dem G’. University of Texas, bars 17–22: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude2.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A letter to Liszt
cues.text: On 16 December 1854, Wagner writes to Liszt of his planned Tristan: “I shall erect a memorial to this loveliest of all dreams”. He imagines a work in which love, from first note to last, can finally have everything it wants.
cues.evidence: Wagner to Franz Liszt, 16 December 1854, quoted in Robert W. Gutman, Richard Wagner: The Man, His Mind and His Music, p. 163; quotation and letter date reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde.

cues.title: A look stops Isolde
cues.text: The melody known as ‘the glance’ carries a scene from the opera. Isolde stands over the wounded Tristan with his sword. He looks into her eyes, and she cannot kill him.
cues.evidence: University of Texas, analysis of the glance motif and its Act I dramatic origin: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude2.php. The sword and wounded Tristan appear in the Act I narrative, summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde.

cues.title: Strings climb under held notes
cues.text: The strings grow quicker as the wind phrases lengthen. Violin and viola runs climb beneath notes held by oboes, clarinets and horns. Small swells keep passing through the orchestra; each fresh rise begins with another instrument already in motion.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 6–10, the extended central ascent: repeated wind phrases, lengthened notes and increasingly rapid string figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Short phrases fill the orchestra
cues.text: The woodwind’s rising semitones and the glance melody now sound together across the orchestra. Brass reinforce them while the strings rush upwards. Material that began with a few exposed notes has become almost too large for the phrase to hold.
cues.evidence: University of Texas, Prelude part 4, annotated bars 74–83: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude4.php. Breitkopf score, pp. 10–12, approach to rehearsal C.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An E beneath the fragments
cues.text: The brass fall silent. The timpani roll softly on E while short string phrases and wind notes emerge from the retreating orchestra. Wagner asks the music to slow gradually. The opening’s hesitant voice is close again.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 12–13, after rehearsal C: E timpani roll, withdrawn brass, string fragments, ‘allmählich im Zeitmass etwas zurückhaltend’. University of Texas, return of the opening material in bars 94–106: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude5.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two singers become the lovers
cues.text: At the Munich première on 10 June 1865, a married couple sing the lovers: Ludwig and Malvina Schnorr von Carolsfeld. Hans von Bülow conducts. Wagner’s completed score has waited six years for these voices and this stage.
cues.evidence: Tristan und Isolde, composition completed in 1859; première history and cast, 10 June 1865, Munich, conducted by Hans von Bülow: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde. The present Fulda recording is an orchestral concert version, identified as ‘Konzertfassung’ in its Commons metadata.

transitions.title: The violins join the broken phrases
transitions.to: A · The strings join the phrases
transitions.how: The violins carry the rising melody into a longer phrase. Violas and cellos begin moving beneath it, and the bass changes note while the upper lines continue. The semitone steps of the opening survive, but the rests no longer separate every attempt. On the following rise, Wagner keeps the violins on their dark G strings.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 3–4, connected string writing and ‘auf dem G’ directions; University of Texas, annotated bars 17–22, https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude2.php.

transitions.title: The brass leave an E behind
transitions.from: C · The whole orchestra presses upwards
transitions.how: The violins rush down from the climax. Brass notes end, the bass thins out, and a quiet timpani roll holds E beneath the smaller wind and string phrases. Wagner marks a gradual slowing of the pulse. The long rising line breaks into short utterances again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 12–13, after rehearsal C: falling violin runs, withdrawal of brass, E timpani roll and ‘allmählich im Zeitmass etwas zurückhaltend’. The separate concert-ending transition is omitted because the performed ending edition is unidentified.

composer.epithet: He hid the orchestra beneath the stage at Bayreuth and taught it to remember everything his characters wanted to forget.
facts: Theodor Weinlig, Leipzig, 1831; then the daily work of provincial opera houses
Dresden court conductor, 1843–49 · Bayreuth Festival founder, 1876
Wrote his own librettos; published essays on theatre, music and politics
Thirteen completed operas, including the four evenings of the Ring
composer.background:
In 1839 Richard Wagner and his wife Minna fled Riga ahead of their creditors and took a storm-battered ship to London. He was twenty-six, an opera conductor with two completed operas and no success worth mentioning. The sea passage stayed with him. A story by Heinrich Heine about a captain condemned to sail for ever became Der fliegende Holländer; its overture begins over a bare fifth, with horns and bassoons calling across the strings’ storm. The Wagners went on to Paris, where he made arrangements for publishers and tried to persuade somebody to stage his music.

He had grown up inside the theatre. Born in Leipzig in 1813, he lost his father as an infant and moved with his mother into the household of Ludwig Geyer, an actor and painter in Dresden. Wagner wanted to write plays before he knew how to write music. Weber’s Der Freischütz and Beethoven’s symphonies supplied the sounds; Theodor Weinlig supplied counterpoint lessons in 1831. Jobs followed in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga. Die Feen remained unperformed, and Das Liebesverbot, his operatic version of Measure for Measure, collapsed after one performance in 1836. That year he married Minna, an actress.
